```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)
```

## Data

The UCI Wine Quality dataset (red wine, 1,599 samples, 11 physicochemical
measurements plus a quality score from 0 to 10). The file is downloaded on
first run if it is not already in `data/`.

```{r load-data}
data_path <- "data/winequality-red.csv"
if (!file.exists(data_path)) {
  dir.create("data", showWarnings = FALSE)
  download.file(
    "https://archive.ics.uci.edu/ml/machine-learning-databases/wine-quality/winequality-red.csv",
    data_path
  )
}

wine <- read.csv(data_path, sep = ";", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
summary(wine$residual.sugar)
head(wine[, c("residual.sugar", "density")])
```

## Part 1: Two groups (median split)

Wines are split at the median residual sugar (2.2 g/L) into Group A (at or
below the median) and Group B (above it).

```{r median-split}
rs_median <- median(wine$residual.sugar, na.rm = TRUE)
sugar_group <- factor(
  ifelse(wine$residual.sugar <= rs_median, 0, 1),
  levels = c(0, 1),
  labels = c("A (<= median)", "B (> median)")
)
table(sugar_group)
tapply(wine$density, sugar_group, mean, na.rm = TRUE)
```

**Null hypothesis.** H0: mu_A = mu_B. Mean density is the same in both groups.

```{r median-boxplot}
boxplot(density ~ sugar_group, data = wine,
        main = "Density by residual sugar (median split)",
        xlab = "Group", ylab = "Density")
```

The median and interquartile range for Group B sit above Group A, so the null
already looks unlikely from the plot.

**Test.** Welch two sample t test, which does not assume equal variances.

```{r welch-t}
t_res <- t.test(wine$density ~ sugar_group, var.equal = FALSE)
t_res

# Same p value computed directly from the t distribution
2 * pt(-abs(t_res$statistic), df = t_res$parameter)
```

**Result.** t is about -14.70 on roughly 1,365 degrees of freedom, with p well
below 0.001. H0 is rejected at any conventional alpha. Wines above the median
residual sugar are denser on average, which points to an association between
residual sugar and density.

## Part 2: Four groups (quartiles)

```{r quartile-groups}
qs <- quantile(wine$residual.sugar, probs = c(0, .25, .50, .75, 1), na.rm = TRUE)
sugar_quartile <- cut(
  wine$residual.sugar,
  breaks = qs,
  include.lowest = TRUE,
  labels = c("A (Q1)", "B (Q2)", "C (Q3)", "D (Q4)")
)
table(sugar_quartile)
```

**Null hypothesis.** H0: mu_A = mu_B = mu_C = mu_D.

```{r quartile-boxplot}
boxplot(wine$density ~ sugar_quartile,
        main = "Density by residual sugar quartile",
        xlab = "Quartile", ylab = "Density")
```

Group medians move upward from A to D.

```{r anova}
aov_fit <- aov(wine$density ~ sugar_quartile)
summary(aov_fit)
p_anova <- summary(aov_fit)[[1]][["Pr(>F)"]][1]
p_anova
```

**Result.** One way ANOVA rejects H0. Density rises steadily across the
quartiles, which strengthens the Part 1 finding. Going to many more groups
(deciles, for example) would not help much here: each group gets smaller, power
drops and the number of comparisons grows. Quartiles are a reasonable balance.

## Part 3: Residual sugar vs. "excellent" wine

A wine is labeled excellent if its quality score is 7 or higher.

**Hypotheses.** H0: sugar quartile and excellence are independent.
H1: they are associated.

```{r chi-square}
excellent <- factor(ifelse(wine$quality >= 7, "yes", "no"), levels = c("yes", "no"))
con_tab <- table(sugar_quartile, excellent)
addmargins(con_tab)

chi_out <- chisq.test(con_tab, correct = FALSE)
chi_out
```

### Permutation check

The chi square p value is checked against a permutation test that shuffles the
excellent labels 2,000 times.

```{r permutation}
set.seed(42)
B <- 2000
obs_chi <- as.numeric(chi_out$statistic)
perm_stat <- numeric(B)

for (b in seq_len(B)) {
  excellent_perm <- sample(excellent)
  perm_stat[b] <- as.numeric(
    chisq.test(table(sugar_quartile, excellent_perm), correct = FALSE)$statistic
  )
}

p_perm <- mean(perm_stat >= obs_chi)
c(chi_square_p = chi_out$p.value, permutation_p = p_perm)
```

**Result.** Both tests give p of about 0.14 (chi square 0.139, permutation
0.137), so independence is not rejected at alpha = 0.05. Residual sugar is
strongly tied to density but shows no meaningful link to whether a wine is
rated excellent.
